newsitem.title: THAILAND: Opposition leaders blast Thai PM as debate begins.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leaders blast Thai PM as debate begins.

text.p: Key opposition leaders accused Thailand's prime minister of condoning corruption and mismanaging the economy as a long-awaited no-confidence debate against him started in parliament on Wednesday.
A grim-faced premier Banharn Silpa-archa listened impassively as opposition leader and former prime minister Chuan Leekpai of the Democrat Party launched the attack.

"The prime minister is guilty of mismanaging the country, irresponsibility, lack of vision, turning a blind eye to corruption in his coalition and abusing power for personal gain," said Chuan in his opening address.
"From now on, the prime minister has lost the legitimacy to run the country as he will only bring damage to the nation and the democratic parliamentary system," he said.
Outside parliament, thousands of pro-Banharn supporters, who had showered the premier's car with flowers as he drove up to parliament, lined the street to lend him moral support.
The televised debate on the opposition-launched no-confidence motion against Banharn was expected to last three days. Banharn was to reply later.
In their motion, the opposition accused him among other things of incompetence, economic mismanagement and plagiarism related to his master's thesis.

Banharn, whose six-party coalition has been in power for 14 months, has denied the accusations and vowed to defend himself in parliament. "I am 100 percent confident," he said on Tuesday when asked about his chances of surviving the debate.
His coalition controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament and political analysts expected Banharn to win the vote despite speculation that there might be cracks in his coalition.

"The six coalition parties will remain together until the vote. After that will be another matter," said Montri Pongpanich, leader of the coalition Social Action Party, after a coalition meeting late on Tuesday.

Political analysts said big changes to government could come after this debate. Banharn could trigger a major cabinet reshuffle to appease critics and accommodate troublesome coalition partners or quit and hand over his post to another more acceptable politician in the coalition, they added.

Banharn's administration has been hurt by an economic slowdown, sluggish exports growth, a battered stock market that sank last week to near three-year-lows and a run on the baht by offshore investors after devaluation rumours.

Banharn has also been plagued by political infighting within the coalition over cabinet posts and factionalism within his core Chart Thai Party. The local media has been hostile against him from the outset.

"The stock market has been battered during your government. We have said from the outset that the men you chose for your economic portfolios were not suitable for their jobs," opposition leader Chuan said.

Chatichai Choonhavan, who heads the Chart Pattana Party, the second largest opposition party, said Thailand used to be a leading Southeast Asian economy in the past but this was not so after Banharn took over.
"Our national debt has soared to US$80 billion and our future generations may not be able to repay," he added.
